A dynasty that ruled much of the Deccan, the plateau of central India, from about the late 2nd century BCE to the early 3rd century CE. The Puranas call them the Andhras. When their rule began is disputed; scholars' estimates run from about 230 to about 30 BCE.

They rose in the space left by the Maurya Empire and held lands in today's Maharashtra, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh. Their capitals included Pratishthana (Paithan) and, later, Amaravati on the Krishna river.

Key points:

  • Their great rivals were the Western Satraps, Saka rulers of western India. Around the early 2nd century CE Gautamiputra Satakarni defeated them and restruck their coins with his own name.
  • They issued many coins, some showing ships, a sign of sea trade. Western ports such as Sopara and Kalyan traded with the Roman world.
  • Though the kings were Brahmanical, they and their subjects gave generously to Buddhism. Inscriptions record their craftsmen carving the gateways of the Great Stupa at Sanchi. The stupa at Amaravati, the prayer hall at Karla and the early caves at Ajanta date from their time.
  • Their court used Prakrit, not Sanskrit. An anthology of Prakrit love poems is credited to King Hala.

The dynasty broke up in the early 3rd century. Its lands passed to several successors, including the Vakatakas in the north and, in the southeast, families that had served them as governors. The Pallavas were one of these.
